claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation during sustained creep loading in FCC/BCC HEA multilayer coatings is governed by the interplay between interfacial dislocation activity and interfacial short-range-order evolution.
Stable short-range order at highly coherent interfaces suppresses dislocation nucleation.
Suppression of dislocation nucleation by stable interfacial short-range order delays creep.
Disruption of interfacial short-range order creates localized stress concentrations.
Localized stress concentrations caused by disrupted short-range order promote dislocation accumulation and accelerated plastic deformation.
The proposed starting coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The baseline interfaces have high coherence and intact short-range-order clusters.
Changing substrate temperature and deposition rate can produce samples with different interfacial coherence and short-range-order states.
Atom probe tomography and synchrotron X-ray scattering can directly quantify the relevant interfacial short-range order.
Compositional complexity and lattice distortion in HEAs affect the balance of deformation processes at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial dislocation accumulation acts as a weak-link mechanism that drives progressive plastic deformation.
Samples with disrupted short-range order will begin creeping earlier than baseline samples with intact short-range order.
Samples with reduced interfacial coherence will begin creeping earlier than highly coherent baseline samples.
Disrupted-short-range-order or reduced-coherence samples will develop a higher interfacial dislocation density than the baseline.
Disrupted-short-range-order or reduced-coherence samples will form localized shear bands relative to the baseline.
Baseline samples with high interfacial coherence and intact short-range order will show minimal dislocation activity and delayed creep onset.
The proposed mechanism applies from room temperature to approximately 0.6 times the melting temperature under stresses of 60–70% of yield strength.
At more extreme temperatures or stresses that induce phase transformations or severe microstructural instability, other deformation mechanisms may predominate.
